speaker: Tom Mueller
title: Impulse Space CEO Tom Mueller - Propulsion, and Rocket Engines - NSF Live
question: In commercial spaceflight, why use a high-thrust chemical transfer stage instead of electric ion propulsion to move satellites from low Earth orbit to geostationary orbit despite electric propulsion's much higher efficiency?
guest: We are eliminating ion thrusters really, because the standard way to get to GEO right now is to go to GTO, geosynchronous transfer orbit, and then use electric propulsion to round out the orbit and take out the inclination—about 1,500 to 1,800 meters per second left. Even with tens of kilowatts of power, that still takes six to eight months, and that is your highest-revenue period, the first part of the mission. Operators are in a hurry to get up there and start earning revenue. To do it from LEO and have to do 4,200 meters per second is actually worse, because you are not doing Hohmann transfers—you are spiraling up, which is not efficient, and you are going through the Van Allen radiation belts. Now you have to design your spacecraft to survive the worst radiation environments on the way, so it just would not make sense. What we are doing is getting you there in a day, in two burns: a GTO burn, and then a second burn that takes out both inclination and circularizes. In six or eight hours you are on station, commissioning your spacecraft and earning revenue.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The short answer is time: chemical stages trade propellant efficiency for speed, and speed is often worth more commercially.

A chemical stage delivers its thrust in minutes-long burns, so a satellite reaches geostationary orbit in hours to days. Electric thrusters produce only fractions of a newton, so the same transfer takes roughly three to six months or more. That delay has several costs:

- **Lost revenue:** a geostationary communications satellite can earn millions of dollars per month, so months of orbit-raising defer income and prolong financing and insurance costs.
- **Radiation exposure:** a slow spiral spends weeks to months inside the Van Allen belts, degrading solar arrays and electronics, which forces extra shielding and array margin.
- **Operational risk:** the long spiral repeatedly crosses crowded orbital regimes, raising collision-avoidance burdens and requiring months of continuous mission operations.
- **Power limits:** electric thrust scales with available electrical power, so heavy payloads need very large solar arrays to keep transfer times tolerable.

Some customers, such as military or time-critical missions, also simply need rapid deployment. Electric orbit-raising is nonetheless increasingly common where operators accept the delay in exchange for lighter, cheaper launches.

models.answer: Although electric ion propulsion achieves far higher fuel efficiency than chemical rockets, its tiny thrust—often measured in millinewtons—forces a satellite to spiral slowly outward over several months rather than completing a chemical transfer in hours or days. In commercial spaceflight, transit time directly affects profitability: reaching geostationary orbit months sooner lets operators begin generating service revenue immediately while reducing financing, ground-operations, and insurance costs. Furthermore, a slow spiral keeps the spacecraft inside the Van Allen radiation belts for months instead of hours, exposing solar arrays and electronics to severe cumulative radiation that degrades power output, demands heavier shielding, or shortens the satellite's operational lifespan. Continuous low-thrust spiraling also requires substantially more total delta-v than impulsive chemical burns near perigee because it cannot efficiently exploit the Oberth effect, and it demands high electrical power that smaller satellites may lack. Consequently, commercial operators choose high-thrust chemical transfer stages whenever rapid deployment, early revenue, and hardware longevity outweigh the launch-mass savings of electric propulsion.

The main reason is time. A chemical stage can complete the transfer in hours or a few days. An ion thruster produces only a fraction of a newton, so the satellite spirals slowly outward and takes about 4 to 8 months to reach geostationary orbit, and longer if it starts from low Earth orbit. A communications satellite can earn hundreds of millions of dollars over its life, so months of delay mean lost revenue, later service starts and more financing and insurance cost.

The slow spiral also keeps the satellite in the Van Allen radiation belts for months, which degrades solar arrays and electronics and shortens its useful life. Continuous low thrust also needs more total velocity change than a two-burn chemical transfer, and the long transfer adds months of ground operations and more chances for something to fail. Thrust is limited by available electrical power, so a satellite would need very large solar arrays to move quickly.

In practice the industry often combines the two. Fully electric satellites like Boeing's 702SP start from a launcher's transfer orbit rather than low Earth orbit, and many satellites use chemical propulsion to get to orbit quickly and electric thrusters for long-term station-keeping.

Although electric ion propulsion uses far less propellant due to its high specific impulse, its extremely low thrust forces a satellite to spiral slowly from low Earth orbit to geostationary orbit over several months—often six months or more—rather than hours or days with a high-thrust chemical stage. For commercial operators, that delay directly postpones revenue generation, increases financing costs, and can jeopardize regulatory deadlines for bringing orbital slots into use.

A slow spiral also keeps the spacecraft inside the Van Allen radiation belts far longer, degrading solar arrays and electronics and forcing heavier shielding or oversized power systems to compensate. In addition, low-thrust transfers suffer higher gravity losses and cannot exploit the Oberth effect the way impulsive chemical burns do, increasing total delta-v requirements. When time-to-orbit, radiation exposure, and rapid revenue recovery outweigh launch mass savings, a chemical transfer stage—or a hybrid chemical-electric approach—remains the more economical choice.

A chemical transfer stage uses more propellant, but its high thrust can put a satellite on a geostationary transfer orbit in minutes. The satellite then coasts for several hours before a second burn can circularize its orbit. Ion propulsion gets much more thrust over time from each kilogram of propellant, but the spacecraft’s available electrical power limits its instantaneous thrust. Raising the orbit can therefore take months.

For a commercial operator, reaching geostationary orbit sooner means the satellite can enter service and earn revenue sooner. A fast transfer also reduces the time its electronics and solar arrays spend in Earth’s radiation belts. Chemical propulsion makes economic sense when those benefits outweigh the cost of launching the extra propellant.
